titulo.texto: Nicolás Moreno’s Murals of the Otopame Peoples

frase_gancho.texto: Two landscapes face each other: one of drought and one of rain.

puente_narrativo.texto: We leave the highlands and climb into the northern sierra of Puebla. Look for a giant crown, round like a sun, made of rays of colored paper, ribbons, and feathers, used in a dance.

guion_corto.texto: These two landscapes were painted by Nicolás Moreno, one of Mexico’s great landscape painters, born in the capital in 1923. He made them between 1963 and 1964, while the museum was being prepared. One shows the Valle del Mezquital in Hidalgo, a dry land of agaves, mesquite trees, and prickly pear cacti, with Otomi huts. The other is a green landscape of the State of Mexico, with cornfields, maguey plants, and adobe houses under a stormy sky. Placed face to face, they read as a pair: the dry season and the rainy season. Moreno also painted the valley of Teotihuacán, for another hall of the museum. Through them, the highlands appear as a place that changes with the year.

guion_largo.texto:
One looks like a land waiting for the rain, and the other, a land that has already received it. They are two landscapes by Nicolás Moreno, placed face to face. Together they tell a whole year of the highlands: the dry season and the rainy season.

Moreno was born in Mexico City on December 28, 1923, and died on February 4, 2012. According to his biography, as a child he traveled the countryside with his grandfather, who drove pack mules. That way of looking at the landscape stayed with him all his life. He studied at the Escuela Nacional de Artes Plásticas and began teaching in 1951. Today he is considered the heir of two great landscape painters, José María Velasco and Dr. Atl.

With Dr. Atl begins an anecdote. His real name was Gerardo Murillo, and Atl means “water” in Nahuatl. He was the great painter of the volcanoes of the Valley of Mexico. When this museum was being prepared, he was invited to paint the valley of Teotihuacán. He said he no longer felt he had the strength, and asked that it be given to Moreno, whom he admired. So Moreno painted three murals for the museum: the one of Teotihuacán, for the Teotihuacán Hall, and the two here.

Look first at the Valle del Mezquital, in Hidalgo, which you already know for its ixtle and maguey. In the foreground, slabs and gravel of limestone stand out. There are also agaves of the kind called lechuguilla, scattered mesquite trees, and prickly pear cacti. Otomi huts can be seen. Over the sierras, rain clouds gather, some black and others white.

The other painting is green. According to the same study, it shows cornfields and a row of maguey plants. There are two adobe houses with reddish roofs, under a gray sky heavy with storm. At the 1964 inauguration it was recorded as “Landscape of the Toluca Valley.” Today INAH identifies it as a landscape of Juchitepec, a town in the State of Mexico. Whatever its name, it is the green face of the highlands.

They face each other to heighten the contrast between fertile soil and dry soil. The agaves of the Mezquital are relatives of the maguey that you saw turned into ropes and blankets. The cornfields in the other painting depend on the summer rains, just like the cycle of the milpa that you already know. The art critic Teresa del Conde wrote in 1997 that the artists who, like Moreno, had to paint landscapes achieved the best works. A museum of anthropology also shows the place where people live.

Moreno worked for the museum between 1963 and 1964, while the building was being raised. In 2012, a few months after his death, INAH paid him a tribute in the lobby of this hall. It was held next to two of his murals.

Before going on, compare the two landscapes calmly. Look for the sky, the ground, and the houses in each one. A landscape also tells how people live in a place: what they must protect themselves from, what is planted, and when the water arrives.

texto: Look for the agaves and prickly pear cacti among the pale rocks of the dry landscape
Find the row of maguey plants and the adobe houses in the green landscape
Compare the two skies: in which one is the storm approaching?

texto.Author: Nicolás Moreno (1923-2012)
texto.Works: “Landscapes of the Mezquital” and “Landscape of the Toluca Valley” (now identified as “Landscape of Juchitepec”)
texto.Subject: the dry land and the rainy land of the highlands

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Valle del Mezquital is a desert where it never rains.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a semiarid region with scarce rainfall that comes mostly in summer; Moreno’s mural shows it with rain clouds over the sierras.
